gov_just_details: In January 2021, while speaking at a rally in Waziristan, Prime Minister Imran Khan announced that 3G/4G internet services will be restored in the district from that day. He said at the ceremony, “I spoke to my security agencies […] we agreed that we need to be cognizant of terrorists using [3G/4G] facility. Despite this, we also thought that it is the need of our young people and that is why this service will become operational from today.”
gov_ack_quote:
In pursuance of Government’s vision of providing internet services across the country, after review of security situation by concerned forums, data services have been restored in District Kurram.

It is pertinent to mention that data services have been restored in six (6) out of seven (7) districts of Erstwhile FATA.

It may be further added the the restoration of data services will help residents to fulfill their educational, health, commerce and communication needs.
telcos_involved: Pakistan: Jazz (Global Telecom), Pakistan: PTCL, Pakistan: Qubee (Augere), Pakistan: Special Communications Organization, Pakistan: Telenor, Pakistan: Wateen Telecom (Abu Dhabi), Pakistan: wi-tribe, Pakistan: Zong (China Mobile)
users_targeted: Students, people need healthcare during COVID, and small businesses
users_target_detail: While many students staged protests to demand internet access for online classes, a student of National University of Modern Languages (NUML) petitioned the Islamabad High Court (IHC) in April 2020 to restore access in former FATA. The IHC ordered PTA to enable 3G/4G broadband internet as a response, but the Federal Government sought more time to assess security conditions before the restoration. The Court, at the time, said, “This is not occupied Kashmir, therefore people of these areas are free to exercise their constitutionally guaranteed fundamental rights.” It further observed, “It appears that there is no refusal on part of the Federal Government to extend the internet facilities to the inhabitants of [FATA] […]. However, it appears that due to the exceptional conditions that had prevailed in the past, the respective Governments and the Pakistan Telecommunication Authority may require time to develop the infrastructure in some affected areas.”

Internet and landline shutdown in the state of Jammu and Kashmir to ensure security and peace before scrapping Article 370 of the Indian constitution that provided special status to Jammu and Kashmir. "Mobile and broadband Internet services were suspended in Jammu and Kashmir on August 4. This was accompanied by heavy deployment of local police and contingents of paramilitary forces. Curfew under Section 144 was imposed in Kashmir and various political leaders including Mehbooba Mufti, Omar Abdullah and Sajad Lone were put under house arrest. Widespread panic prevailed as families were not been able to reach their friends and family on the phone (mobile and landline).

On 17 August, 2G services were restored in 5 districts of Jammu i.e. Jammu, Samba, Kathua, Udhampur and Reasi . However they remained suspended in Poonch, Rajouri, Kishtwar, Doda and Ramba.

2G services were were also restored in 35 police stations and landlines under 17 telephone exchanges were restored in Kashmir Valley.

On 18 August, ban on 2G services that were started in parts of Jammu was restored. According to a news source phine internet services were restored in Doda, Kishtwar, Ramban, Rajouri and Poonch districts on 28 August.

As of August 30, phone lines are active in Jammu but Kashmir valley continues to face even phone communication blockade.

By 13 September, landlines were made fully functional in Jammu and Kashmir."

However, independent reports and anonymous sources confirmed that the internet was deliberately cutoff through orders by the Kenyan government to disconnect circuits at sea cable landing stations.

event: The internet was shutdown in Kenya from 13:30 to 20:45 (UTC+0) on Jun. 25 as evident by severe disruptions from multiple measurement sources. Authorities went back on their word not to shutdown the internet, and ISPs denied or contradicted themselves after the shutdown had occurred. According to indepedent and anonymous sources, Kenyan authorities ordered the tampering of subsea cable landing stations in order to shutdown the internet, which gave the appearance of a cable cut which are common in the region. Since they couldn't differentiate between inland circuits, four other countries had severe internet disruptions at the same time as well: Burundi, Rwanda, Tanzania, and Uganda. event: After the military council announced they would seize Starlink devices, local businesses hosting access points in Mohnyin, Kachin State complied around Nov. 18, shutting down this avenue for internet access for locals. After a protracted shutdown of traditional internet and phone service which had been mostly ongoing for months since July across Kachin State, many cities started providing Starlink so people could have access to the internet. By announcing the seizure of Starlink devices with knowledge that people used them to access information and communicate using the internet, and given the context of past deliberate shutdowns of traditional internet providers in the area, the junta intentionally disrupted the internet. Rather than directing ISPs to follow a shutdown order, the junta instead threatened other local businesses who were acting as de facto ISPs to stop providing the service. (There had been reports of arrests of people providing Starlink in the country in 2024).

By Aug. 20, some mobile connections started to be restored in parts of Kachin. Myitkyina was still cutoff as of Sep. 13 as locals tried to connect with IP Star and Starlink. However, the regime was inspecting local businesses for satellite connection nodes and making arrests in the process. The shutdown was still prevalent across Kachin State as of Oct. 3 and Nov. 18. Connections were restored on Mytel in Bhamo around 4:00pm (local time) on Dec. 2. Myitkyina regained partial access to MPT service by Jan. 6, 2025, and some other townships (like Danai City) had MPT, Ooredoo, and Atom service in certain neighborhoods, but most of Kachin State had been undergoing a shutdown for 6 months as of Jan. 21, 2025 as fighting was ongoing between the Kachin Independence Army (KIA) and junta. By Jun. 17, 2025, Mytel mobile service returned to Myitkyina. As of Jun. 25, 2025, the following townships had service available: Myitkyina (Mytel, Atom), Hpakant (MPT), Puta-O (Ooredoo, Atom), Khaung Lan Phu (MEC), and Naungmon town had some MPT, with the rest Kachin state offline. The state reached one-year of a shutdown on Jul. 21, 2025. Mohnyin had Mytel mobile service return on Sep. 9, 2025. The state reached 15 months of a shutdown on Oct. 21, 2025. Puta-O had Mytel service return by Oct. 28, 2025. The state reached 16 months of a shutdown by late Nov. 2025.

Neighboring Central African Republic (CAR) also experienced a disruption between 3:30am and 6:30pm (UTC+0) on the same day, and both countries had connectivity return relatively quickly, supporting the notion that the Cameroon branch of the WACS cable was tampered with given the CAR's downstream reliance on internet coming through sub cables via Cameroon. actual_cause_details: There were multiple platform blocks of remaining unblocked platforms ahead of Election Day, continuing in the following weeks due to ongoing protests and information control
event: Alongside the full network shutdown between Oct. 29 and Nov. 3, authorities in Tanzania imposed multiple platform blocks in the lead-up to and following Election Day, targeting apps that weren't already blocked under existing orders (Grindr, Clubhouse, X, and Telegram). According to OONI data, WhatsApp was blocked from Oct. 29 to Nov. 6, Signal was blocked from Oct. 28 to Nov. 4, FB Messenger was blocked between Nov. 3 and Nov. 4. TikTok was blocked Oct. 28 and still remains inaccessible. The blocks were initially applied inconsistently across providers, and only the ongoing block of TikTok seems to be uniformly applied after Nov. 3 as evident by nearly 100% of OONI measurements returning as anomalies per day. Similar to the full network shutdown, these blocks coincided with mass killings of protestors and serious human rights abuses by Tanzanian authorities, and the one that remained in effect in early December was likely continued in anticipation of Dec. 9 protests. The TikTok blocking finally ended by Dec. 29.

event: Beginning Dec. 29, Iranian authorities imposed hyper-localized disruptions and throttling in areas of Bushehr, Ilam, Isfahan, Fasa, Mashhad, Sanandaj, Shiraz, and Tehran where anti-regime protests were quickly expanding. These shutdowns affected primarily mobile networks, with fiber connections also degraded in places like Isfahan, with service unusable for either some or all of the day, and with access limited to just the domestic intranet. In this period, security forces began their crackdown on largely peaceful protesters with unlawful use of force and firearms, as well as mass arbitrary arrests, which resulted in the killing of at least 28 protesters and bystanders, including children, in 8 provinces beginning Dec. 31.
